Marlin 1894C .38 Special / .357 Magnum

Another new gun that I picked up at the same time as my Chiappa Rhino 60DS Revolver: A Marlin 1894C in .38 special / .357 Magnum.

It's a lever-action rifle, but it has a confluence of features not found anywhere else. Not in the "original" lever action (i.e. the Henry), or the classic lever-action (the Winchester 1894) or present-day imitators (the Rossi R92), or modern-day takes on the lever gun (Browning's BLR):

  1. Gate-fed integrated magazine
  2. Ejection port on the side
  3. Receiver already drilled & tapped to have a proper accessory rail attached

Honestly, Browning's BLR is probably the pinnacle of lever-rifle efficacy (it uses a box magazine and can therefore be made to accept bullets with pointy tips which will travel farther, faster, with better ballistics), but there's something about the side gate that and "tactical" reload capability that captivated me.

Why .38 special / .357 magnum? Because that's a very common (but capable) revolver round, and the classic "cowboy" aesthetic requires a revolver and rifle that can fire the same cartridges... and while this can also be found in .44 special / .44 magnum (indeed, I witnessed a fellow purchase the .44 special/mag Marlin 1894 on Black Friday at Cabela's for something like $400), .38/.357 rounds are significantly cheaper.

Something something Zombie Apocalypse I think a gate-fed lever gun is actually a solid choice in a zombie-survival scenario:

  1. Common cartridge (in fact, it can shoot two different cartridges!) means you'll be able to have usable ammo for longer after mass-production ceases.
  2. Gate-fed means you can top-up whenever you have a chance, without ever having to detach a magazine and take the rifle out of readiness - crucial when the living dead could attack at any moment.
  3. Ability to mount a scope means it can be used at longer ranges (than other lever guns) - which increases your ability to procure food and gives you more lead time to flee if you judge you won't be able to dispatch every one of the undead (or the living who may want to take your stuff).
  4. Relatively simple action (manual, lever-operated) may remain serviceable for longer periods of time between cleanings and in harsher conditions than more complex actions - who knows when you'll be able to stop fleeing the undead hordes and clean up?
  5. Relatively simple action means that almost anyone can operate it - if you have to hand it to a relative stranger or untrained family member, there are no fiddly bits, it's just 1.) move lever 2.) pull trigger.

Marlin was bought by Remington around a year and a half ago (if I recall correctly), and Remington discontinued the .38/.357 Model 1894 carbine. I'd been keeping my eyes out for a "deal" on one (MSRP $700ish, selling on GunBroker.com post-discontinuation for ~$1400) that whole time (with an outstanding back-order on file at my local gun store) and I finally found one in acceptable condition at an acceptable price point!

Photos

  1. Zoomed Out
  2. With Ammo that I Shot
  3. Booty Shot
  4. (the) Action Shot

Scope

I went for a Leupold LR Duplex, which is adjustable from 4x to 12x optical zoom and has adjustable focus - solid and clear, but no bells or whistles. It's decent; haven't had a chance to test it out beyond a 25 yard indoor range.

Performance

My Henry is so smooth to operate. The Marlin is so rough and resistant to motion - but that might be exacerbated by the fact that I hadn't yet cleaned it after I bought it. From handling other Marlins previously, this lack-of-smoothness was not unexpected. We'll see how much I can improve it after a thorough cleaning and lubrication.

Shoots straight, though! I took it to the range the day after I bought it and discovered that the ironsights were totally acceptable for ranges that my naked eye could see, and, well, the scope's adjustable so I'd've had to mount it all wonky for that to not line up.

As any review on the internet will tell you, a lever rifle barely kicks at all when loaded with .38 special and it's only slightly more pronounced than firing a .22LR. A pleasant surprise was shooting the Hornady LeverRevolution .357 magnum rounds. LeverRevolution is a line of bullets in calibers usually made with flat noses and used in pistols, but that also have rifles made for them - so they make a pointier tip and a heavier powder load so the bullet will go faster and farther for longer, out of a longer rifle barrel. They kicked like a beast (my shoulder and hand were bruised) compared to every other round I shot - .38 or .357 - including the "Bear Load" Magnums! I cannot wait to try them at 50 and 100 yards... makes me wish I owned a chronograph.
